findings.problem: File I/O (std::fs) is imported and used inside a function that also does parsing and domain construction. I/O, parsing, allocation, and domain construction are fused together in a single function, making it impossible to test core logic without real filesystem access.
findings.failure_mode: Cannot reason about or unit-test parsing logic in isolation; every call requires a real file on disk; side effects are unpredictable and untestable.
findings.fix: Split into a shell function that reads the file and a pure parsing function that accepts &str or &[String]. Move fs::read_to_string into the shell; keep the core logic pure and deterministic.

findings.problem: fs::read_to_string(path).unwrap() — unwrap() on a fallible file read. Panics if the file is missing, unreadable, or too large.
findings.failure_mode: Untrusted input (file path) causes the entire process to abort instead of returning a typed, recoverable error.
findings.fix: Return Result<Vec<Record>, LoadError> and use .map_err(|e| LoadError::Io(e))? instead of unwrap().

findings.problem: parts[1].parse::<u32>().unwrap() — unwrap() on a fallible parse. Panics if the value field is not a valid integer.
findings.failure_mode: Malformed CSV data causes a panic instead of returning a typed ParseError, violating panic freedom.
findings.fix: Use .map_err(|_| ParseError::Invalid)? and return a typed error enum instead of unwrap().

findings.problem: as u16 — lossy cast from u32 to u16. Values outside 0..=65535 silently truncate.
findings.failure_mode: Out-of-range values silently wrap to incorrect domain values, producing invalid records with no error or diagnostic.
findings.fix: Use u16::try_from(value).map_err(|_| ParseError::Overflow)? for a checked, fallible conversion.

findings.problem: parts[0] and parts[1] — unchecked indexing into a Vec produced by split+collect. If a line has fewer than 2 comma-separated fields, this panics with an index out of bounds panic.
findings.failure_mode: Malformed input lines (empty, single-field, or whitespace-only) panic at runtime via bounds check failure instead of returning a typed error.
findings.fix: Use line.split_once(',').ok_or(ParseError::Invalid)? to parse two-field records without indexing. Bind as (_name, value_str) and parse value_str directly.

findings.problem: Record{name: String, value: u16} — raw primitive String and u16 fields. No domain invariants enforced at the type level. Any caller can construct a Record with an empty name, negative-appearing value (via overflow), or otherwise invalid state.
findings.failure_mode: Illegal domain states are representable; name and value constraints are invisible to the type system, so callers can create invalid Records directly.
findings.fix: Replace with a parse-boundary smart constructor: newtype Name(String) validated at construction (non-empty, bounded length), and use a bounded u16 or a value enum. Provide Record::new(name: Name, value: Value) -> Result<Record, ParseError> as the only constructor.

findings.problem: println!("loaded {}", parts[0]) — logging/side effect embedded inside the data-parsing closure. Pure calculation code must not produce I/O.
findings.failure_mode: Parsing logic has observable side effects, making it impossible to call deterministically; output ordering and presence affect test results and downstream behavior.
findings.fix: Remove println! entirely from the parsing logic. If logging is needed, the shell layer should log after calling the pure parser, or the parser should return a result the shell can log.

findings.problem: let parts: Vec<String> = line.split(',').map(...).collect() — allocates a Vec of Strings for every line without any capacity bound or domain cap. Additionally uses split+collect instead of split_once for a two-field record, and the outer collect() into Vec<Record> has no try_reserve or max-items validation.
findings.failure_mode: Malicious or extremely large input files cause unbounded memory allocation with no cap, leading to OOM or denial of service.
findings.fix: Validate a domain cap (max lines) before allocation, use Vec::new() then values.try_reserve(max_items).map_err(|_| Error::Allocation)?, and use line.split_once(',') per line to avoid per-line Vec allocations.

findings.problem: The entire function load_frames performs file I/O (fs::read_to_string), parsing (split/parse), logging (println!), domain construction (Record {..}), and result collection (collect()) in one monolithic function. There is no Data/Calculations/Actions separation.
findings.failure_mode: Cannot test pure parsing logic without a filesystem; cannot reason about side effects; violates the mandatory functional-core imperative-shell architecture.
findings.fix: Extract a pure fn parse_lines(input: &str, max_items: usize) -> Result<Vec<Record>, ParseError> for calculations. The shell fn load_frames(path: &str) -> Result<Vec<Record>, LoadError> handles only I/O and delegates to the pure parser.

findings.problem: The function returns Vec<Record> with no Result type. All fallible operations (file read, parse, bounds check, allocation) are collapsed into panics via unwrap() instead of a typed error enum.
findings.failure_mode: Callers have no way to distinguish between IO failures, parse errors, overflow, allocation failures, or malformed input — all manifest as panics.
findings.fix: Define enum LoadError { Io(std::io::Error), Invalid(String), Overflow, Allocation } and return Result<Vec<Record>, LoadError>. Map each fallible operation to the appropriate variant.
